source: ASME B16.34-2025, Tables 2-1.1 through 2-3.19, SI units. Transcribed from a purchased copy held outside version control.
note: A VALVE IS NOT RATED BY THE FLANGE STANDARD. flange-pt-ratings holds B16.5 and B16.47, which rate FLANGES; this pack holds B16.34, which rates VALVES. The two agree on Standard Class by construction and differ everywhere else: B16.34 adds a SPECIAL CLASS with higher allowable pressures for valves that pass extra NDE, adds Class 4500, and does not carry Class 400 at all.

conventions.ratingClassIsNotPressureClass: Two different words both called "class". PRESSURE CLASS is 150/300/.../4500. RATING CLASS is Standard, Special or Limited and says how much examination the valve has had. A Class 300 Special valve and a Class 300 Standard valve are the same pressure class with different envelopes.
conventions.noClass400: B16.34 tabulates 150, 300, 600, 900, 1500, 2500 and 4500. Class 400 is absent, though B16.5 has it. A PMS line naming a Class 400 valve is not answerable from this standard, and that is a real answer, not a gap.
conventions.class4500IsValveOnly: Class 4500 exists here and in no flange standard this repo holds. Nothing in flange-pt-ratings can answer for it.
conventions.limitedClassIsComputed: Limited Class (Mandatory Appendix V) is not tabulated - it is derived per valve from a stress-area calculation. It is named in ratingClasses so a consumer can refuse it explicitly rather than treating it as absent data.
conventions.siIsCanonical: Only the SI tables are transcribed. The U.S. customary tables are the same curves re-rounded; holding both would give one question two answers.

observations.note: Transcribed as printed. The two sections of one table do not share a temperature list, so a Special Class valve in this group cannot be rated where a Standard Class one can.

At these cells the Special Class figure is 0.1 bar BELOW the Standard Class one. Both sections have converged on the same allowable stress and the two roundings fall either side of it. It is printed that way; it is not a licence to treat Special as weaker.

Group 1.18 (9Cr-2W-V steel) and group 3.19 (N06230 nickel alloy) are printed with an identical Standard Class curve from 38 C to 600 C, diverging at 625 C and above. Recorded because it looks like a copy-paste fault in this pack and is not one - and because each group's suspected typo is contradicted by the other, which is what makes both anomalies callable.

anomalies.evidence: Three independent checks say 160.6 bar where the SI table prints 106.6. (a) B16.5-2025 group 1.18 at 500 C class 1500 is 160.6. (b) B16.34 Table 2-1.18C, the U.S. customary twin, gives 2,380 psi at 900 F, which is 5.01x its own class 300 figure - the 5x step the column keeps at every other temperature. (c) B16.34 group 3.19, printed with the same SI curve as 1.18 from 38 C to 600 C, reads 160.6 in this cell. 106.6 is a digit transposition.

The column runs 304.7 bar at 425 C and 286.3 bar at 475 C; the printed 205.9 at 450 C is far outside that interval and would make the curve non-monotonic. B16.5-2025 group 3.19 gives 295.9, which sits between the neighbours, and B16.34 group 1.18 - printed with the same SI curve up to 600 C - also reads 295.9.

The column falls 450.0, 442.3, then prints 462.2 at 538 C before falling again to 421.7 at 550 C - a rise no rating curve makes. Class 4500 is exactly 1.8x class 2500 in every other row of this table, and 236.8 x 1.8 = 426.2. The printed 462.2 transposes the middle digits of 426.2.

The column falls 550.3, 542.6, then prints 587.7 at 425 C before falling to 530.4 at 450 C. Class 4500 is 1.8x class 2500 throughout the table, and 299.3 x 1.8 = 538.7; the U.S. customary twin gives 7,795 psi at 800 F, which is 537.5 bar. 587.7 transposes 538.7.

corroboration.note: B16.34 Standard Class is meant to reproduce the flange ratings for the same material group, and it does so in 99.7284% of comparable cells. Every disagreement is listed below rather than averaged away.

seatRatingRule.text: "The valve pressure-temperature rating shall be the lesser of the shell rating or the seat and seal rating." The shell comes from ASME B16.34 Standard Class (clause 4.2); the seat from Table 1 (clause 4.3).
seatRatingRule.whyItMatters: THE PLATFORM HAS BEEN OVER-RATING SOFT-SEATED BALL VALVES. A Class 600 shell in group 1.1 is 102 bar at 38 C. The same valve with a PTFE seat above DN 100 is 19.7 bar - a factor of five. Reading the shell rating alone and calling it the valve rating is the single largest over-statement this pack can make.
seatRatingRule.appliesTo: BALL valves with PTFE or R-PTFE seats (API 608 Table 1, keyed by ball design and DN band) and CATEGORY B BUTTERFLY valves with the same seats (API 609 Table 1, keyed by pressure class). The two standards key the same idea on different axes, which is why a seat curve carries a discriminators object rather than fixed fields.
seatRatingRule.metalSeatedIsNotHere: Table 1 covers PTFE and R-PTFE only. A metal-seated ball valve is not limited by this table, and the pack says nothing about it rather than implying the shell governs - that is a different clause of API 608 and is not transcribed.
seatRatingRule.categoryAButterflyIsNotHere: API 609 Table 1 is headed "for Category B Valves". A CATEGORY A butterfly valve has no ASME class rating at all - clause 1.2 a) makes it manufacturer-rated cold working pressure - so neither a shell rating nor a seat rating can be looked up for one. Asking this pack for it is a category error, and the pack says so rather than returning a Class 150 figure that was never claimed.
seatRatingRule.noPtfeAtClass600: API 609 Table 1 gives Class 600 an R-PTFE column and no PTFE column. The standard does not rate PTFE there; that is an answer, not a missing cell.
